context: Festival Scenes is a pair of small six-panel folding screens made in Japan during the Edo period (1615-99), painted with ink, color, gold, and gold leaf on paper. The Cleveland Museum of Art says they appear to depict one festival but are actually a series of separate scenes, including sumo, juggling, a float with musicians, a dance circle, courtiers playing kickball, and a theater performance.

descriptions.k: Look at all the fun! People dance in a circle. Others juggle and play music. Can you find a game? Which part would you join?
descriptions.g12: This pair of folding screens shows a festival in Japan long ago. There are dancers, musicians, jugglers, and games. It looks like one big party, but each part is a different scene. Which scene would you visit first?
descriptions.g35: These small folding screens were painted in Japan between 1615 and 1699. They seem to show one festival, but they are really many separate scenes: sumo, juggling, musicians on a float, a dance circle, a kickball game, and a theater show. Gold makes them glow. Why might an artist put so many scenes into one picture?
descriptions.g68: Festival Scenes is a pair of small six-panel folding screens from the Edo period. They appear to show one festival, but they are actually a series of separate scenes: sumo, juggling, a float with musicians, a dance circle, courtiers playing kickball, and a theater performance. How does gold and the screen format help join separate scenes into one lively view?
descriptions.g910: Made in Edo-period Japan (1615-99), Festival Scenes are a pair of small folding screens in ink, color, gold, and gold leaf. They seem to depict one festival but combine separate scenes of sumo, juggling, a musicians' float, a dance circle, courtly kickball, and theater. How does the screen format let the painter combine many entertainments into a single, shifting view?
descriptions.g1112: Festival Scenes (Edo period, 1615-99) are a pair of small six-panel screens in ink, color, gold, and gold leaf that appear to portray a single festival but actually assemble separate entertainments: sumo, juggling, a float with musicians, a dance circle, courtly kickball, and theater. How does the format collapse time and place into one composite spectacle, and what does this reveal about how Edo-period viewers enjoyed and curated images of public life?

teacherNote.context: Festival Scenes are a pair of small six-panel folding screens made in Japan in the Edo period (1615-99) in ink, color, gold and gold leaf on paper. The museum says the screens appear to show one festival but are really separate scenes, including sumo, juggling, a float with musicians, a dance circle, kickball and theater.
directions: Have students divide a long strip of paper into panels and draw separate scenes of one event, then discuss how to link them.
Ask students to choose one small scene and describe what is happening using details they can see.
Discuss why an artist might show entertainments from different places and times together.
